newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Koreans in fear of more man-made disasters.
newsitem.headline: S.Koreans in fear of more man-made disasters.

text.p: Families of the 502 people who died when a South Korean department store collapsed two years ago vowed on Sunday to fight the government, which they say is not doing enough to prevent further disasters.
In the country's worst man-made disaster, Seoul's multi-level Sampoong Department Store collapsed like a house of cards on shoppers during an evening sale.

In a ceremony marking the disaster's second anniversary, victims' families said a similar tragedy was unavoidable because corrupt local government officials continued to turn a blind eye to poor construction.
"Nothing has changed in the past two years, and corruption which caused Sampoong to collapse still prevails at the highest levels," said Min Jung-eui, who represents victims' families.
Min's 20-year-old daughter was one of those crushed to death under the rubble.
"Until corruption is cleaned up and the government makes sure companies don't cut corners on construction and safety, we can expect other disasters to follow," he said.
Jun Byoung-chul, father of another victim, said: "I am sorry my daughter's death and all the other deaths have not brought about change for safer construction."
Store owner Lee Joon is currently serving a 7-1/2 years in jail for criminal negligence. The store's structural problems were known before the collapse but kept secret from customers and staff.
The victims' families said they would set up a commission to survey major construction sites across the country to prevent similar disasters from occurring.

The government has pledged to step up enforcement of safety regulations in public works, but several smaller accidents and reports of faulty construction showed the country was still not completely safe.
In April, a U.S. firm commissioned to examine the safety of a 1.74 trillion won ($1.95 billion) project to build a high-speed rail line found serious defects.
A report by Wiss, Janney, Elstner Associates Inc said five of the 37 bridges examined in the project linking Seoul and the southern city of Pusan had structural and safety problems.
Families of Sampoong victims also pointed to the collapse of a retaining wall last month at a Seoul apartment complex that killed one person and injured six.
"Many apartment complexes being built these days on hills are especially dangerous," said Jeong Seok, a researcher at the city-funded Seoul Development Institute.
"Contractors try to pack too many units on the land which is supported by extremely high foundation walls," he said.
Jeong said he believed about half of apartment complexes being erected in redevelopment projects in Seoul were built or being built without proper safety precautions.
Disasters also loomed underground. In 1994, an underground gas explosion at a subway construction site in the southeastern city of Taegu killed 100, many of them children.
A similar blast took place in Seoul last April after workers accidently severed an underground gas pipeline at a subway construction site.

Contractor Ssangyong Engineering and Construction blames inaccurate pipeline maps, authorised by the Seoul City Gas Co Ltd, for the mistake, while the gas company rejects the charge that its maps contained faulty information.
"Seoul City Gas maps showed the pipeline was three metres away from the construction site, but in fact it was located 1.5 metres away from the site," said Ssangyong official Kim Hun-dong.
Kim said such mistakes were common because maps are frequently inaccurate. "A map needs to be re-drawn to show the exact location of the pipes," he said. ($1 = 888.10 won)
